title: After the Victory: Rome, the Rhine and Alexandria
sum: Vitellius is dead, and Rome learns that winning a civil war is not the same as peace. The soldiers hunt the losers, the Senate heaps honors on Vespasian (who is far away in Egypt), and Mucianus quietly takes charge in the city. The Senate's old quarrels return: Helvidius Priscus against Eprius Marcellus, and a first trial of the informers who served Nero. The Capitol, Rome's chief temple, is cleared and its foundation stone laid on 21 June.

Out on the Rhine, Julius Civilis, a Batavian noble and Roman officer, uses Vespasian's name to start a revolt of his own. It spreads to Gaul, the Roman camps fall, and a Gallic "empire" is sworn to at Novesium, until Petilius Cerialis breaks it. Near the end of the book, at 4:81-84, Vespasian waits at Alexandria for the sailing season and heals a blind man and a man with a damaged hand, and Tacitus tells how the god Serapis came to the city. The book ends with Domitian held at Lugdunum and not allowed to reach the war.
readings: A year of fear after victory: soldiers, senators and generals all try to turn the war to their own use, while a frontier people sees Rome's weakness and acts. Tacitus's own eye is on character and how power corrupts it.

Many of the places and offices are those of the Gospels and Acts: Syria, Cyrene, Alexandria, proconsuls and procurators, taxes, Caesar. The two great events of AD 70, Rome's temple of Jupiter rising and Jerusalem's temple falling, stand side by side at 4:53 and in Josephus.

Three ancient writers tell that Vespasian healed two men there. The Gospels have their own healings with spit and a withered hand. Scholars read the Alexandria story as politics, as an ordinary recovery, or as something more; the notes at 4:81 give each.

views.C: A Christian reads Book 4 with the Bible's Rome beside it. The Bible's God sets up and holds ruling powers ("There is no authority that does not come from God," Romans 13:1), yet the apostles hold that "Obeying God has to come before obeying people" (Acts 5:29). Marcellus (4:8) and Helvidius (4:7) stand for two ways of living under a bad emperor. The Capitol's rebuilding (4:53) and Jerusalem's burning (Josephus, War 6.4.5) are the same summer. At Alexandria (4:81) the Gospels' healings with spit and a withered hand (Mark 8:23; Mark 3:5) are answered differently: Mark shows no doctor's opinion asked, and Jesus takes the man out of the village (Mark 8:23; Mark 8:26).
views.H: Historians have three ancient accounts of the Alexandria healings (Tacitus, Suetonius, Dio) and one of Domitian's Gaul story that disagrees with the other two (Josephus, War 7.4.2, against Tacitus and Suetonius, Domitian 2.1). John Meier, as quoted by John Dickson, reads the healing as a staged show that gave Vespasian legitimacy; Eric Eve reads it as Flavian propaganda that Mark answered. For the Rhine, the Histories as we have it breaks off at 5:26, before the end of the war.
views.R: The Roman world of Book 4: a Senate that still debates but fears; consuls who take office on 1 January; the Praetorian Guard and the legions as makers of emperors; informers who take rewards; the grain supply from Africa and Egypt; the Capitol's rites by soothsayers, Vestals and a pontiff; the oaths of soldiers and senators; and Alexandria, whose god Serapis the Greek kings brought from Sinope.
views.J: Josephus tells much of the same time: the Capitol's burning and Sabinus's death (War 4.11.4), Vespasian in Alexandria (War 4.10.5-6; War 4.11.5), Titus's march to Jerusalem (War 4.11.5), the German revolt (War 7.4.2), the Sarmatian raid (War 7.4.3), the triumph (War 7.5.6) and the tax to Jupiter Capitolinus (War 7.6.6). The Gospels and Acts share places (Cyrene, Alexandria, Pontus, Asia, Illyricum), offices (proconsul, procurator, praetorium) and customs (lots, oaths, vows, taxes). Josephus says nothing of the healings at Alexandria.

deep.h: How Tacitus knows what he tells
deep.b: Tacitus does not often name his sources in Book 4, but the text shows how he treats them. At 4:49 he says that no one was present at the private talks of Piso and Festus, so the truth is "unknown". At 4:61 he reports a hard story with ferebatur, "it was said". At 4:83 he gives the Serapis story as what "the Egyptian priests" tell and says that Roman writers had not yet explained the god. At 4:81 he says the healings are still told by the people who were there "now that there is nothing to gain from lying". The speeches of Civilis, Cerialis and Vocula are given in his Latin; whether they preserve the speakers' words or his version of their case, he does not say.

deep.h: The Bible's people, places and customs in Book 4
deep.b:
By verse, the main links (each is argued in the verse notes; weak ones are marked there as background):

  • 4:2 Praetorian Guard (Philippians 1:13; Philippians 4:22); Domitian, emperor from AD 81 (Revelation, date argued).
  • 4:3 Judea, Syria, Illyricum and Spain (Luke 2:2; Romans 15:19; Romans 15:24); Lucilius Bassus in Josephus (likely).
  • 4:4 Mucianus of Syria; triumph (2 Corinthians 2:14; Colossians 2:15).
  • 4:5-4:8 Stoics (Acts 17:18); lots (Acts 1:26); duty to rulers (Romans 13:1-7; 1 Timothy 2:1-2; Acts 5:29).
  • 4:10 Asia (Acts 19:10). 4:11 Appian Road (Acts 28:15).
  • 4:14 abuses of the draft (Luke 3:14). 4:15 Caligula's statue plan (Josephus, War 2.10.1).
  • 4:17 Varus (very likely the Syrian governor of Herod's last years); tribute and Judas of Galilee (Acts 5:37; Matthew 22:17-21).
  • 4:28 Claudius (Acts 11:28; Acts 18:2). 4:38 and 4:52 grain ships (Acts 27:6; Acts 27:38).
  • 4:39 King Agrippa and Berenice (Acts 25:13; very likely the same). 4:41 oaths (Matthew 5:34).
  • 4:42 emperors named in the New Testament. 4:44 exile to islands (Revelation 1:9). 4:45 Cyrene (Mark 15:21; Acts 13:1).
  • 4:48-50 proconsul and procurator (Acts 13:7; Acts 18:12); Festus (not the Festus of Acts 24:27).
  • 4:51 Titus sent to Jerusalem (Luke 21:20; Matthew 24:2); Parthians (Acts 2:9).
  • 4:53 Capitol and Temple (Ezra 3:12; Haggai 2:9; Matthew 17:24).
  • 4:54 Druids' prophecy (Deuteronomy 18:22). 4:55 ruler as god (Acts 12:22).
  • 4:58 Jupiter as Zeus (Acts 14:12). 4:60 siege famine (2 Kings 6:25).
  • 4:61 hair vow (Numbers 6:18; Acts 18:18); prophetess (Judges 4:4; Luke 2:36).
  • 4:81 spit and a withered hand (Mark 8:23; Mark 3:1-5); witnesses (1 Corinthians 15:6); public cures of the lame (Acts 3:1-10; Acts 14:8-12). 4:82 Josephus's prophecy (War 3.8.9). 4:83 dreams (Genesis 41:8); Alexandria and Pontus (Acts 18:24; Acts 2:9). 4:84 idols (Acts 19:35; Psalm 115:4-8).

deep.h: The healings at Alexandria: four ways to read them
deep.b:
As a Roman story. Tacitus presents it as showing "heaven's favor." Suetonius and Dio tell it too (Vespasian 7.2-3; Dio 65.8). The three differ on the second man's ailment (a hand, a leg, a withered hand).

As staged. John Meier, quoted by John Dickson, calls it a "photo opportunity"; Dickson judges it probably a fraud. Eric Eve argues it is Flavian propaganda that Mark answered by adding spit to the blind man of Bethsaida (Mark 8:23).

As an ordinary recovery. Tacitus's own doctors said the blind man's sight "hadn't been eaten away" and the hand's joints "could be made whole."

As a sign with a source. The Bible gives tests for signs: Deuteronomy 13:1-3 (what the sign asks you to worship), Matthew 24:24 and 2 Thessalonians 2:9 (signs can serve a lie). This is a Christian reading of the Bible's tests, and no named scholar is cited for it here.

What the Gospels add: Mark shows no doctor's opinion asked, the critics in John cannot deny the cure (John 9:30-33), and Jesus is not made emperor by it.

deep.title: Why the healings sit at the end of the Gaul story
deep.b: Claude's reading: Tacitus places the Alexandria passage (4:81-84) between the Gallic empire's collapse and Domitian's stalling at Lugdunum. In the West a Gallic "empire" is sworn to and falls; in the East a god is said to confirm the new emperor. Tacitus then tells us where the god came from, as if the reader should weigh the sign before trusting it.

echoes: Mark 8:22-26; Mark 3:1-5; John 9:1-7; Acts 28:15; Acts 5:37; Luke 3:12-14; Luke 21:20-24; Matthew 22:17-21; Matthew 17:24-27; Romans 13:1-7; Acts 5:29; Matthew 5:33-37; Ezra 3:10-13; Haggai 2:3-9; Deuteronomy 18:22; Judges 4:4; Acts 18:18; Acts 14:11-15; Genesis 41:8; Acts 27:6; Acts 11:28; Philippians 1:13; Mark 15:21; Acts 25:13; Acts 3:1-10; Acts 14:8-12

settings.what: Vespasian's letter to the Senate
settings.when: after the news of Vitellius's fall, at the start of the year
settings.why: To act as an emperor without waiting to be named one: modest about himself and confident about the state, though it still read as if the war were going on.
settings.readers: Roman readers of the Histories, who knew what an emperor's letter to the Senate was for and could hear the tone of a man still far from the city.

settings.what: Mucianus's letters to the Senate
settings.when: as he came toward the city
settings.why: To claim credit for putting Vespasian in power while holding no office, and to tell the Senate how to treat Vitellius. Senators resented the tone and hid it behind flattery.
settings.readers: Roman readers, who knew Mucianus as the strong man in Rome and could judge the tone of letters from a governor who held no office in the city.

settings.what: Helvidius Priscus: choose the envoys by their character
settings.to: the Senate, with Marcellus in the room
settings.when: in the debate on sending envoys to Vespasian
settings.why: To keep the informers of Nero's reign away from the new emperor's ear and to turn the Senate's vote into a judgment on character.
settings.readers: Roman readers, who knew choosing envoys by lot as an old custom and would hear Helvidius's speech as a challenge to it.

settings.what: Eprius Marcellus: let lots choose, and put up with the emperor you have
settings.by: Eprius Marcellus, who had accused Thrasea Paetus under Nero
settings.to: the Senate, Helvidius and the consul-elect
settings.when: in reply to Helvidius
settings.why: To avoid being singled out as unfit, to defend the old custom of lots, and to say that a survivor of Nero's reign bows to whoever rules.
settings.readers: Roman readers, who knew Marcellus's record under Nero and could weigh his claim to have served out of fear.
views: he served Nero out of fear, not choice (4:8)
the Senate must say whom the emperor may trust (4:7)

settings.what: Musonius Rufus's charge against Publius Celer
settings.when: at the hearing that set the trial for the next day
settings.why: To charge that Celer had trapped Barea Soranus with false testimony, which tested whether the Senate would punish informers.
settings.readers: Roman readers, who knew the name of Soranus and would take the charge as the first test of how the new regime treated the informers of Nero's reign.

settings.what: Julius Civilis at the sacred grove
settings.by: Julius Civilis, a Batavian noble and an officer of Rome
settings.to: the chiefs of the Batavians and their boldest men, at a night feast
settings.when: as the draft for Vitellius's army was being enforced
settings.why: To turn anger at draft abuses into a rising and to persuade them that Rome was too weak to punish it, since either outcome could be explained to Vespasian as service to him.
settings.readers: Roman readers, who saw Batavians as subject allies. Tacitus gives the rebel a full speech, so they hear the complaint against Rome in Latin.

settings.what: Civilis's appeal to the Gauls
settings.by: Julius Civilis, in private talks and gifts
settings.to: Gallic leaders, and the cohorts he had captured
settings.when: after the first victory over the Roman fleet and cohorts
settings.why: To make the Gauls partners in the revolt by calling tribute slavery and holding up the Germans' past victory over Varus.
settings.readers: Roman readers, who saw Gauls as subjects. They hear Civilis's case against tribute in Rome's own language, and Cerialis answers it at 4:73-4:74.

settings.what: The Batavian cohorts' message to Herennius Gallus
settings.when: as they came near the camp
settings.why: To say they meant no harm unless blocked, which let them claim the battle that followed was self-defense.
settings.readers: Roman readers, who knew the winter camps and the ranks of legates and would see in this message a threat dressed as politeness.

settings.what: The legions' answer to Civilis
settings.by: the two legions in the Old Camp
settings.when: when asked to swear to Vespasian
settings.why: To refuse a traitor's oath and keep faith with Vitellius, their emperor to the last.
settings.readers: Roman readers, who knew what an oath to an emperor meant to a soldier and would weigh the legions' loyalty to a dead cause.

settings.what: The soldiers' complaint against Hordeonius Flaccus
settings.by: the Roman soldiers on the march
settings.when: as Vocula's column moved to relieve the camp
settings.why: To turn their anger at a sick, hated general into a charge of treason, which is how mutiny started.
settings.readers: Roman readers, who knew how a mutiny began and would recognize the charge of treason as its usual spark.

settings.what: Hordeonius Flaccus's reading of the letters
settings.to: the soldiers at Bonna, with their eagle-bearers
settings.when: after the soldiers blamed him for the defeat
settings.why: To prove he had begged for help through Gaul, Britain and Spain; by handing the letters to the eagle-bearers first, he let the army hear its news before its commanders, which Tacitus calls a very bad precedent.
settings.readers: Roman readers, who knew the legion's eagle and its bearer and would see in this order the start of the army's habit of acting on its own.

settings.what: Civilis's reply to Montanus
settings.to: Alpinius Montanus, a cohort prefect from the beaten side, sent to stop the war; Tacitus does not say by whom
settings.when: after Montanus came to tell him to stop the war
settings.why: To win Montanus over by listing Rome's wrongs against him and by promising freedom to those who dare.
settings.readers: Roman readers, who knew Montanus as a Roman officer sent to talk the rebel down and now hear what the rebel said back.

settings.what: Domitian's first speech in the Senate
settings.when: on the day he first took his seat in the Senate
settings.why: To seem modest and to propose honors to Galba's memory; his blushes passed for modesty.
settings.readers: Roman readers, who lived under Domitian's later reign (Tacitus wrote after his death) and would read the blushes with that knowledge.

settings.what: Junius Mauricus asks for the imperial records
settings.when: after Publius Celer was convicted and the signal for revenge on informers was given
settings.why: To let the Senate see the emperor's records so it could learn who had asked for which prosecutions; Domitian answered that the emperor must be consulted.
settings.readers: Roman readers, who knew the informers by name and would see Mauricus's request as a threat to many of them.

settings.what: The senators' oath against informing
settings.by: the magistrates and then every senator, in turn
settings.when: as part of the purge of Nero's informers
settings.why: To clear the guilty from the innocent by an oath that only the innocent could swear plainly.
settings.readers: Roman readers, who knew the Senate's ways and the oaths of office, and who knew informers by name.

settings.what: Curtius Montanus against Aquilius Regulus
settings.to: the Senate, with Messalla pleading for his brother Regulus
settings.when: at Regulus's hearing
settings.why: To keep informers from slipping off with their wealth and to call the Senate back to its duty: punish informers while the memory of the tyrant is fresh.
settings.readers: Roman readers, who knew Regulus as an informer under Nero and would hear Montanus's warning that tyranny comes back.

settings.what: Vipstanus Messalla's plea for his brother
settings.by: Vipstanus Messalla, too young to be a senator
settings.when: at the same hearing
settings.why: To protect his brother by standing in the danger himself, which moved some senators. Tacitus praises the family loyalty.
settings.readers: Roman readers, who valued family duty (pietas) and would take Messalla's plea for his brother as honorable.

settings.what: Marcellus: "We leave you your Senate"
settings.to: Helvidius Priscus and the Senate, with Domitian present
settings.when: as Helvidius pressed the attack on him
settings.why: To threaten to walk out and force the Senate to choose between the quarrel and its respect for the Caesar present.
settings.readers: Roman readers, who knew the quarrel between Helvidius and Marcellus and the Senate's fear of losing either man.

settings.what: Domitian's opening plea
settings.when: at the next Senate meeting
settings.why: To urge that grief, anger and the harsh necessities of earlier times be put aside.
settings.readers: Roman readers, who knew Domitian's later reign and would hear this call to forget as one that suited those with something to forget.

settings.what: Mucianus speaks for the informers
settings.when: at the same meeting
settings.why: To speak at length in favor of the informers and to warn, in gentle and pleading tones, those who were reviving cases they had started and dropped; the senators gave up the freedom they had begun to use.
settings.readers: Roman readers, who knew Mucianus held the real power in Rome and would see how a mild-sounding plea silenced a Senate.

settings.what: Manlius Patruitus's complaint
settings.when: at a hearing held by the old rules
settings.why: To complain that he had been beaten in the colony of Sena and mocked in a staged funeral, and to win punishment for those who did it.
settings.readers: Roman readers, who knew that a senator's person was meant to be safe and would see the hearing as a moment when the Senate acted like itself.

settings.what: Mucianus to the Vitellianist soldiers
settings.to: the surrendered Vitellianist soldiers, almost stripped of gear, and the victors
settings.when: as the soldiers were separated by army
settings.why: To end their fear that this was a massacre, tell them they served the same emperor, and prepare their absorption into the Praetorian Guard.
settings.readers: Roman readers, who knew what happened to a beaten army and would feel the soldiers' fear of a massacre.

settings.what: Claudius Sagitta's warning to Piso
settings.by: Claudius Sagitta, prefect of the Petrian cavalry wing
settings.when: after reaching Africa by a quick voyage, ahead of the centurion Mucianus had sent
settings.why: To tell Piso that an order to kill him had been given, that his cousin and son-in-law Galerianus was dead, and that his only hope was bold action; Piso was not moved.
settings.readers: Roman readers, who knew Piso's family and the fate of Galerianus and would read Sagitta's warning as an offer to start another civil war.

settings.what: The centurion's greeting of Piso as emperor
settings.by: the centurion Papirius, sent by Mucianus
settings.to: Piso and the crowd at Carthage
settings.when: on reaching the port of Carthage
settings.why: To draw Piso into a show of ambition that could be charged against him; when Piso questioned him, he found that the centurion had been looking for a charge and a way to kill him.
settings.readers: Roman readers, who knew how a cheer could be a trap and would watch the crowd and Piso handle it.

settings.what: Piso's edict at Carthage
settings.when: after the centurion's cheers and the crowd's shouts
settings.why: To calm a city that had hailed him as emperor and keep himself from looking like a rival.
settings.readers: Roman readers, who knew a proconsul of Africa could be hailed as a rival and would read the edict as a man frightened for his life.

settings.what: Titus's plea to Vespasian
settings.when: before sailing for Judea
settings.why: To ask his father not to believe accusers about Domitian, since a large family guards a ruler better than legions.
settings.readers: Roman readers, who knew the Flavian family and, writing after Domitian's reign, knew what became of the brothers' quarrel.

settings.what: Helvidius's prayer at the Capitol
settings.by: Helvidius Priscus as praetor, with the pontiff Plautius Aelianus dictating
settings.to: Jupiter, Juno, Minerva and the gods who guard the empire
settings.when: at the laying of the first stone, 21 June
settings.why: To ask the gods to prosper the rebuilding and lift up, with their help, the homes human devotion had begun for them.
settings.readers: Roman readers, who knew the Capitol's rites, the pontiff and the praetor's role, and whose own state religion this prayer belongs to.

settings.what: The Druids' prophecy that rule would pass to the peoples beyond the Alps
settings.by: the Druids, the priests of the Gauls
settings.when: after news of the Capitol's burning reached Gaul
settings.why: To read the Capitol's fire as a sign of heaven's anger and to foretell that mastery of human affairs would pass to the peoples beyond the Alps.
settings.readers: Roman readers, who knew the fire and the Gallic sack of the city long ago, and who hear Tacitus call the prophecy empty superstition.
views: he calls it "the empty superstition of prophets" (4:54)
the Gallic empire's armies were beaten by Cerialis (4:71-4:79)

settings.what: Vocula to the Gallic rebels
settings.to: Classicus and Tutor and their followers
settings.when: as they camped apart from the Roman legions
settings.why: To warn the Gauls that Rome had crushed Sacrovir and Vindex and would crush them, and that Galba's easing of their tribute had put hostility into them.
settings.readers: Roman readers, who knew the earlier Gallic revolts of Sacrovir and Vindex and would hear Vocula use them as warnings.

settings.what: Vocula's last speech to his soldiers
settings.to: the Roman legionaries at Novesium, with their officers
settings.when: after the Gauls bought off centurions and soldiers
settings.why: To shame the soldiers into refusing the oath to Gaul, and to pray to Jupiter and Quirinus that the camp not be defiled.
settings.readers: Roman readers, who knew Jupiter Best and Greatest and Quirinus as the city's own gods and would hear the prayer as a Roman's last appeal.

settings.what: Veleda's prediction of German success
settings.by: Veleda, a maiden of the Bructeri
settings.when: before the legions were destroyed
settings.why: To foretell the Germans' success and the destruction of the legions; when it came true her authority stood at its height.
settings.readers: Roman readers, who knew the Germans as a people with prophetesses and goddesses and who hear Tacitus call the custom a superstition that grows.

settings.what: The legions' lament on the day of the march
settings.by: the soldiers of the 16th legion and its surrendered auxiliaries
settings.when: in the days before the set day to leave Novesium
settings.why: To voice their fear and shame at a march ordered by those they had made masters of their life and death.
settings.readers: Roman readers, who knew what it meant for a legion to march out under the enemy's orders and would feel the disgrace.

settings.what: The Tencteri's message to the Agrippinenses
settings.by: the boldest of the Tencteri's envoys
settings.to: the council of the city of the Agrippinenses
settings.when: after Civilis and Classicus took the legions
settings.why: To demand that the city pull down its walls, kill the Romans and share its goods, as the price of alliance with the free Germans.
settings.readers: Roman readers, who saw a Roman colony in Germany as theirs and would hear the German demand to tear down its walls as an outrage.

settings.what: The Agrippinenses' answer
settings.when: in reply
settings.why: To refuse the demand without saying so, offering instead to lift trade taxes and to submit the dispute to Civilis and Veleda.
settings.readers: Roman readers, who knew the colony as a Roman one and would read its careful answer as that of a city caught between two powers.

settings.what: Civilis to the Tungri
settings.by: Julius Civilis, riding into their column
settings.when: in the narrow pass on the Mosa
settings.why: To switch a whole army by saying the Batavians did not rise to rule other peoples.
settings.readers: Roman readers, who knew the Tungri as an auxiliary people and would see a rebel winning over a whole Roman army with a speech.

settings.what: Valentinus and Auspex at the Gallic assembly of the Remi
settings.by: Julius Valentinus of the Treveri, then Julius Auspex of the Remi
settings.to: delegates of the states of Gaul
settings.when: as the Roman legions came into Gaul
settings.why: Valentinus: to keep the war going with attacks on Rome. Auspex: to show Rome's power and the blessings of peace, and win a vote to lay down arms.
settings.readers: Roman readers, who saw Gaulish assemblies as the place where the empire's loyalty was tested, and hear both sides argued in full.

settings.what: The soldiers' demand to destroy the colony of the Treveri
settings.to: their general Cerialis (Tacitus does not name the person addressed)
settings.when: on entering the colony of the Treveri
settings.why: To get the city burned and its loot taken, as payment for the destroyed camps and by the example of Cremona.
settings.readers: Roman readers, who knew what had been done at Cremona and would weigh the soldiers' appeal to it.

settings.what: Cerialis comforts the shamed legions
settings.to: the legions called in from the Mediomatrici
settings.when: when the armies met
settings.why: To soothe them by saying that what had happened was driven by fate, soldiers' and generals' quarrels, or the enemy's trickery, to count that day as the first of their service and oath, and to forbid anyone to throw mutiny or defeat in a comrade's face.
settings.readers: Roman readers, who knew the shame of the surrendered legions and would hear a general restore them to the army.

settings.what: Cerialis to the Treveri and Lingones
settings.to: the Treveri and Lingones, assembled in their conquered colony
settings.when: after the rebel armies were beaten and before he moved on
settings.why: To tell them the empire was built on peace, taxes and the army, and that they should accept obedience with safety over stubbornness with ruin.
settings.readers: Roman readers, who would hear in this speech their own empire's defense of its rule, given to the people it ruled.

settings.what: Civilis and Classicus's letter to Cerialis
settings.when: while Cerialis held the colony of the Treveri
settings.why: To spread the false news that Vespasian had died and to offer him the empire of Gaul or battle; Cerialis sent the letter on to Domitian.
settings.readers: Roman readers, who knew false news of an emperor's death as a weapon and would watch Cerialis send the letter on.

settings.what: The rebels' council of war
settings.by: Civilis and Tutor, with Classicus deciding
settings.when: before the battle at the Treveri colony
settings.why: To decide whether to wait for more Germans (Civilis) or to attack at once (Tutor, who won).
settings.readers: Roman readers, who heard how the enemy argued about waiting or striking and who knew from 4:77 what the choice cost them.

settings.what: Cerialis to his scattered legions
settings.to: the survivors of the legions captured at Novesium and Bonna
settings.when: in the camp, in the middle of the surprise attack
settings.why: To shame the legions into holding the line by taking the blame on himself and telling them they could report the loss to Vespasian.
settings.readers: Roman readers, who knew the shame of the legions captured at Novesium and Bonna and would hear a general rebuild their pride.

settings.what: The blind man's and the sick-handed man's petition
settings.by: a blind man and a man with a sick hand, both of Alexandria
settings.when: while he waited for the summer sailing
settings.why: To ask the emperor to heal them as the god Serapis had directed. For Vespasian it was a public test he could not safely refuse.
settings.readers: Tacitus's Roman readers. The evidence is in the book: at 4:83 he says the origin of Serapis "hasn't yet been made well known by Roman writers"; at 4:50 he says "the troubles we soon suffered", speaking as a Roman who lived through the years he describes; at 4:81 he points to witnesses who "still tell" the healings. That he writes for readers who expect a Latin history to cover such things is an inference from these lines, not something he says. The surviving text names no patron or dedicatee for Book 4.
views: John Meier, as quoted by John Dickson, calls it a 'photo opportunity' that gave a new ruler legitimacy; Eric Eve reads it as Flavian propaganda (see the verse notes).
the petitioners acted on a dream-order from Serapis; the doctors judged the cures possible; witnesses still tell the story.

settings.what: Serapis's answer through the name Basilides
settings.by: the god Serapis, as Vespasian read it
settings.when: in the god's temple, when he asked about the empire
settings.why: To answer Vespasian's question without words: he took Basilides's appearance as a divine sign and read the force of the response from the name.
settings.readers: Roman readers, who knew omens and dreams as part of public life and who hear Tacitus tell it without comment.

settings.what: The Egyptian priests' story of Serapis
settings.by: the priests of Egypt, as Tacitus reports them
settings.when: as an account of the god whose temple Vespasian had just entered
settings.why: To give the origin of a god that, Tacitus says, Roman writers had not yet explained, and to show where Serapis came from.
settings.readers: Tacitus's Roman readers. He opens the story with "The origin of the god hasn't yet been made well known by Roman writers"; reading that as addressed to readers who expect a Latin history to cover such things is an inference. The surviving text names no patron or dedicatee for Book 4.
views: Plutarch tells of Ptolemy's dream and the Sinope statue with other names (Isis and Osiris 28).

settings.what: The youth's command in Ptolemy's dream
settings.by: a youth of extraordinary beauty, as the Egyptian priests tell it
settings.when: while he was adding walls, temples and rites to the newly founded Alexandria
settings.why: To order him to send his most trusted friends to Pontus to fetch the god's statue, promising the kingdom good fortune and the city that received it fame.
settings.readers: Roman readers, who were told a story "not yet made well known by Roman writers" and who knew dream-commands to kings.

settings.what: The Pythian Apollo's answer to Ptolemy's envoys
settings.when: as they sailed with gifts for King Scydrothemis
settings.why: To say plainly: bring back the statue of his father and leave his sister's behind.
settings.readers: Roman readers, who knew the Pythian Apollo as the Greek world's oracle and would hear his answer as a clear one.

settings.what: The youth's second warning
settings.when: after Ptolemy neglected the matter
settings.why: To announce ruin for him and his kingdom if his orders were not carried out.
settings.readers: Roman readers, who knew that kings who neglected a god's order were punished, and who hear Tacitus say kings are "prone to fear".

settings.what: The threatening figure's order to Scydrothemis
settings.when: after three years of delay
settings.why: To tell him not to delay the god's plans any longer.
settings.readers: Roman readers, who knew a ruler's reluctance to give up a sacred image and would see disasters as the god's pressure.

settings.what: Mucianus's plan to keep Domitian from the front
settings.when: once news came of Valentinus's capture
settings.why: To keep Domitian from sharing the credit or spoiling the peace by sending him to a safe place near the army, not into it.
settings.readers: Roman readers, who wrote and read of Domitian after his reign and would hear Mucianus's reason with that knowledge.

settings.what: Domitian's secret message to Cerialis
settings.when: from Lugdunum
settings.why: To test whether Cerialis would hand over the army if Domitian came; Cerialis treated it as a boy's wish.
settings.readers: Roman readers, who knew Domitian as emperor and would read his early secret move as a sign of his character.
views: Whether the plan was war on his father or money and men against his brother was uncertain (4:86).
Domitian planned a campaign against Gaul and the Germanies that his father's friends talked him out of (Domitian 2.1).

traditions.q: May a Christian take an oath, since Jesus said "do not take oaths at all"?
views: Yes, for grave and right reasons, in truth, judgment and justice. The Church has understood Jesus' words as not excluding oaths of that kind (Catechism 2153-2154), and an oath demanded by an illegitimate authority may be refused (2155).

Yes. The Westminster Confession says an oath is "warranted by the Word of God, under the new testament as well as under the old," to be sworn in God's name only, with holy fear, and only to what the swearer is persuaded is true (22.2-3).
No. The Schleitheim Confession (Article VII) says "we shall not swear at all," because Christ "prohibits all swearing to His (followers), whether true or false."
